papers.title: Identification of mitophagy inducers for Alzheimer's disease via high-throughput endogenous ATP5B tagging system.
papers.summary: This paper describes a new high-throughput screening method that tags ATP5B, a mitochondrial protein, at its natural genomic location in cells to track mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria). Using this system, the researchers screened for compounds that can boost mitophagy, since impaired mitochondrial clearance is linked to Alzheimer's disease. They identified candidate small molecules that act as mitophagy inducers, which could serve as potential therapeutic leads for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.why: This paper is directly relevant because it provides both a methodological tool and candidate compounds for studying and potentially enhancing mitophagy in neurodegenerative contexts, which could inform experimental or therapeutic angles for the PhD project's focus on mitophagy in neurons.
papers.figure: The figure showing the high-throughput screening pipeline and validation of top mitophagy-inducing hit compounds using the endogenous ATP5B tagging system.

papers.title: SUMO-2/3 modification of PINK1 restrains basal mitophagy through MAPL-dependent regulation of mitochondrial surveillance.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how SUMOylation (addition of SUMO-2/3 proteins) to PINK1, a key mitophagy-regulating kinase, affects basal mitophagy levels in cells. The researchers found that the enzyme MAPL adds SUMO-2/3 to PINK1, which suppresses baseline mitochondrial surveillance and limits unnecessary mitophagy. This mechanism helps explain how cells maintain mitochondrial quality control without excessive turnover under normal conditions.
papers.why: Understanding how mitophagy is fine-tuned at baseline levels is directly relevant to studying neuronal mitochondrial quality control, which may differ in interneurons and could be probed using spatial multi-omics approaches.
papers.figure: A figure showing PINK1 SUMOylation status alongside basal mitophagy flux measurements (e.g., mitophagy reporter assays) in MAPL-manipulated cells would be most informative.

papers.title: Emerging Insights into Autophagy-Lysosomal Dysfunction in Age-Related Neurodegenerative Disorders.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how the autophagy-lysosomal pathway, the cell's system for breaking down and recycling damaged components, becomes dysfunctional with aging and contributes to neurodegenerative diseases. It likely covers mechanisms such as impaired lysosomal acidification, buildup of protein aggregates, and failure to clear damaged mitochondria as cells age. The review probably synthesizes recent findings across disorders like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease to highlight common degradation pathway failures.
papers.why: Understanding how autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction develops with age provides essential mechanistic context for interpreting mitophagy defects in aging neurons, directly relevant to the PhD project's core focus.

papers.title: Engineered LC3 molecular switch aids in regulating autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper describes an engineered version of the LC3 protein that acts as a molecular switch to control autophagy, the cellular process that degrades and recycles damaged components. LC3 is a core protein involved in forming autophagosomes, the structures that engulf material destined for degradation, including damaged mitochondria during mitophagy. By engineering LC3 to be switchable, researchers gain a tool to turn autophagy on or off more precisely, likely useful for studying or manipulating this pathway in cells.
papers.why: Since LC3 is central to autophagosome formation in both general autophagy and mitophagy, an engineered switch could serve as a valuable tool for dissecting mitophagy dynamics in neurons within the broader PhD project.

papers.title: The optogenetic tool ASAP acutely inhibits autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper reports that ASAP, a genetically encoded optogenetic voltage/calcium sensor widely used for imaging neuronal activity, has an unexpected side effect of acutely blocking autophagy when activated by light. This finding suggests that researchers using ASAP to monitor neural activity might inadvertently be disrupting cellular degradation pathways in the same cells. The study highlights a potential confound for combining optogenetic imaging tools with autophagy or mitophagy research.
papers.why: Since this project studies autophagy and mitophagy in neurons using advanced imaging and spatial techniques, knowing that a common optogenetic sensor can unintentionally suppress autophagy is critical for designing experiments that avoid confounding results.

papers.title: Phylospatial optimal transport for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data integration
papers.summary: This paper introduces a computational method called Phylospatial Optimal Transport that integrates single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data using lineage/phylogenetic relationships between cells. It leverages optimal transport theory to map cells across different data modalities while respecting their developmental or clonal ancestry. This could help reconstruct spatial context for sequenced cells or predict lineage relationships in spatial data.
papers.why: This method could help the project integrate spatial transcriptomics with single-cell data to map cell lineages and types, including interneuron subtypes, onto spatial brain tissue contexts, which is a core technical need for the research.

papers.title: CROST 2.0: an expanded repository of spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: CROST 2.0 is an updated database that collects and organizes spatial transcriptomics datasets from many studies into one searchable repository. It expands the number of datasets, species, tissues, and technologies covered compared to the original version, making it easier to find relevant data. The resource likely includes tools for browsing, searching, and downloading processed spatial gene expression data for reuse in research.
papers.why: This repository could serve as a valuable source of existing spatial transcriptomics datasets from brain tissue to cross-reference or validate findings related to interneurons, perineuronal nets, and mitophagy-related gene expression patterns.

papers.title: OGS-MA114 ameliorates FUS mutant-associated ALS pathology by activating PINK1-dependent mitophagy.
papers.summary: This paper describes a new compound called OGS-MA114 that helps treat ALS caused by mutations in the FUS gene. The compound works by turning on PINK1, a protein that triggers mitophagy, the process cells use to clear out damaged mitochondria. By boosting this cleanup process, the drug reduces disease-related damage in cells affected by the FUS mutation.
papers.why: This directly relates to the PhD project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, offering a concrete example of a PINK1-dependent pathway that could inform mechanistic or therapeutic angles in neurodegeneration research.
